title: Building a strong culture of error
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino sets out how she plans to build a Teach Like a Champion style culture of error with a difficult bottom-set Year 9 class whose norms had drifted towards open mocking after lockdown and remote learning. The goal is a room where students expect mistakes, are unafraid to admit them and see them as part of learning. Her plan has several strands: establish and rehearse routines from day one with automated entry cues, secure success by explicitly teaching every fact and modelling every task, treat mistakes as shared learning using inclusive language, and watch for the tells of students likely to belittle others. She adds anonymised responses, a warning before Show Call, and early parental contact to shift the class norms. The post is a candid, practical plan rather than a report of results.
points: A culture of error is built slowly through consistent routines, not through a single lesson or occasional use.
Students are more willing to make mistakes when the teacher has provided all the facts, tools and modelling they need to succeed.
Inclusive language such as 'I am glad we made this mistake' rebrands errors as useful learning and depersonalises them.
Pre-empting mocking by spotting students' tells, warning students before Show Call and anonymising weak responses protects anxious learners.
Early phone calls home and discussion with the head of department and head of year are part of shifting entrenched class norms.
quotes: The ultimate goal of such a culture is a classroom where students are not afraid to make or admit mistakes. In such a classroom, mistakes are expected and can be planned for in advance. The level of challenge of a task is acknowledged so students are aware that mistakes are natural and that they are an essential part of the learning process.

Building such a strong culture of error takes time, impeccable planning, and a consistent approach. This (like many other TLAC techniques) is not something that can have a lasting effect if only applied once or sporadically. In fact, it is developed slowly so students know what to expect, eventually accepting and, indeed, welcoming it.

In my year 9 class, there are a significant number of students who mock each other when one of them gets an answer wrong, or loudly compare responses with the aim of belitting their peers. In this class, the norms have started to incorporate negative behaviours where, sadly, students expect open mocking.

I use this to help me teach explicitly so that I explain every single fact that students need to know. I don’t leave them to discover this for themselves. I also explictly teach the connections between facts so students can start to develop schemas in their long term memory.

Mistakes need to be rebranded as a useful learning opportunity rather than as something that is shameful. While students are working independently, a lot of useful data can be collected from student work using Active Observation.

Is a student likely to belittle someone’s response or snigger while someone reads out their answer? If so, it is important to identify students’ tells or pre-empt the mocking negative behaviours by reminding students about expectations before I call on someone to share their answer. As with everything else, if I don’t get students to practice the expected positive behaviours, they are likely to fail.
By then, they will know that their work is selected not to be criticised but to be appraised.
